hook.line: The café has online reviews now, and Tomás has to answer them in writing. Written Spanish dresses up a little: it has its own way to say hello, its own way to sign off, and it keeps *usted* from the first line to the last.
hook.es: Muchas gracias por su comentario tan agradable. Lo esperamos pronto en el café.
hook.en: Thank you very much for your kind comment. We hope to see you at the café soon. (to a man, formal)

examples.en: Could you send me the information? (formal)
Thank you very much for your attention.
I look forward to your reply. (a man writing)
We look forward to hearing from you.

rule:
A message has three parts: hello, the point, goodbye. Spanish picks each one by who is reading.

Hello. To someone you don't know: *Estimado señor Rojas:* or *Estimada señora Rojas:*. Colombian work emails often just open with *Cordial saludo*. To someone close: *Querido* or *Querida* plus the name. The ending matches the reader, not you. After the greeting, Spanish puts a colon where English puts a comma.

The point. Once you start with *usted*, stay there: *su comentario*, *le*, *lo*, *la*. English has one you for everybody, so it never has to choose; Spanish readers notice a switch.

Goodbye. Formal: *Quedo atento a su respuesta* (*atenta* if you're a woman, *atentos* for a team), *Gracias de antemano*. To friends: *Un abrazo*, *Saludos*.

English says Dear to everyone. Spanish never says *Querido* to a stranger.
smallPrint: Teachers call this written register: the fixed openings and closings of letters and emails (*fórmulas de saludo y despedida*).

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *Querido* or *Querida* and type the opening of a letter to your grandmother: *___ abuela:*
yourTurn.why: Your grandmother is a woman, and the greeting matches the reader.

yourTurn.prompt: You're Mariana, closing a formal email. Pick *atento* or *atenta* and type the whole line: *Quedo ___ a su respuesta.*
yourTurn.why: *Atento* describes the writer, so a woman writes *atenta*.

yourTurn.prompt: Open a formal email to Mr Rojas.
yourTurn.why: *Estimado* for someone you don't know, and a colon after the name.

yourTurn.prompt: Write to a customer (formal): Thank you very much for your attention.
Ask a supplier you don't know: Could you send me the information?
yourTurn.why: *Podría* with no *s* is the polite form for *usted*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it formal: *Gracias por tu comentario.*
You're writing for the whole café team now: *Quedo atento a su respuesta.*
yourTurn.why: A team is *we*, so *quedamos*, and *atento* goes plural.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it formal, to a man: *Te esperamos pronto en el café.*
yourTurn.answer: Lo esperamos pronto en el café.
yourTurn.why: For *usted*, *te* becomes *lo* for a man (*la* for a woman).

pitfalls.why: Almost. The greeting matches the person reading, and Mariana is a woman.
*Querido* is for people you're close to; a stranger gets *Estimado*.
You opened with *usted*, so stay there: *su respuesta*, not *tu*.

pitfalls.wrong: Gracias por tu comentario. Lo esperamos pronto.
pitfalls.right: Gracias por su comentario. Lo esperamos pronto.
pitfalls.why: Pick one: *lo* is formal, so *tu* has to become *su* too.

personal: Write a three line email to a hotel or a café you know: a formal greeting, one question with *¿Me podría...?*, and a closing such as *Quedo atento a su respuesta* (*atenta* if you're a woman).
